title: Tubaani
author: Ama Nunoo
desc: Two cups of bean powder with a teaspoon of alkali, wrapped in katemfe leaves and steamed thirty minutes — eaten with shea butter and pepper.
longDesc: Tubaani is steamed bean cake, a northern Ghanaian snack, and the alkali is what makes it work: a teaspoon of ground saltpetre into two cups of bean powder with a tablespoon of salt, mixed with water to a smooth consistency. Spoonfuls are wrapped in katemfe leaves and steamed above boiling water on a splatter guard for thirty minutes. The oldest documented account says the alkali is added to soften the flour, and that it is eaten with shea butter and pepper — which is the detail that makes tubaani northern rather than generic.
ingredients: 2 cups bean powder — black-eyed pea or cowpea flour
1 tsp ground saltpetre — or kanwa, see the note
equipment: Saucepan and splatter guard, or a steamer
steps: In a mixing bowl, mix the bean powder, salt and saltpetre.
Add water and mix to a smooth consistency.
Scoop a spoonful into a katemfe leaf, wrap, and set aside.
Repeat until the mixture is used up.
Bring water to the boil in a saucepan.
Place a splatter guard over the saucepan and carefully arrange the wrapped parcels on it.
Cover and steam 30 minutes, then take off the heat.
Serve with shea butter and ground pepper.
chefTips: The alkali is structural, not seasoning. The 1968 government account says plainly that it is added to soften the flour, and without it tubaani is dense.

The sources name three different alkalis for the same job — ground saltpetre, kanwa described as concentrated salt, and kanwa described as potash. They are not the same chemical and no source reconciles them.
Smooth consistency is the mixing cue. Lumps in the paste become hard spots in the steamed cake.
Katemfe leaves are the documented wrapper. Banana leaf and corn husk also appear across sources; use whatever is pliable and food-safe.
A splatter guard over a saucepan is this author's improvised steamer and it works well — the parcels sit above the water rather than in it.
Shea butter and pepper to serve is the northern way and it is worth doing properly. Shea butter is nutty and slightly bitter against the plain bean cake.
Documented steaming times run twenty, thirty and forty minutes across four sources. Thirty is the middle and the two that agree on it may not be independent.
commonMistakes: Letting the parcels sit in the water rather than above it.
Serving it plain rather than with shea butter and pepper.
sources: Adapted from a tubaani recipe on Face2Face Africa. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'BY Ama Nunoo, 11:55am November 06, 2019'. Yield 'Serves 2 to 4' is SINGLE-PASS.
Ingredients exactly as printed: 2 Cups of Beans Powder; 1 Tsp of Ground Salt Petre; 1 Tbsp of Salt; Katemfe leaves (wrap).

Method verbatim: 'In a mixing bowl, mix beans powder, salt and salt petre. Then add water and mix into a smooth consistency. Scoop a spoonful into a katemfe leaf, wrap and set aside... Bring water to a boil, place a splatter guard on the saucepan, then carefully place the wrapped mixture on the splatter guard and cover to steam.' Then: 'Let cook for 30 minutes and take off heat.'

AN INDEPENDENCE PROBLEM, flagged: this method's wording is NEAR-IDENTICAL to a MAGGI Ghana tubaani page, so one derives from the other and THEY ARE NOT INDEPENDENT SOURCES. The MAGGI page (credit 'MAGGI Ghana', 6 servings, 42 minutes) lists 2 cups beans powder, 1 shrimp tablet, 2 tbsp shrimp powder and 1 bunch spinach, and also says 'Let cook for 30 minutes'. It is internally inconsistent — its ingredient list says shrimp powder while step 1 says 'fish powder', and the spinach is never used in the method.

TWO FURTHER DOCUMENTED VERSIONS, both without quantities. (1) Pulse Ghana, byline as printed 'Berlinda Entsie, 16:17 - 23 March 2023': black-eyed pea or cowpea flour and water, no quantities; 'let it cook for about twenty minutes'; and a useful cue — 'beat... till the mixture becomes fluffy'. (2) Prime News Ghana, byline as printed 'By Fareeda Abdul Aziz, 15 September 2021': Cowpea Flour, Water, Onions, 'Kanwa (Concentrated Salt)', Powdered Pepper, Chilli Pepper, Butter/Cooking Oil, Salt/Powdered seasoning, no quantities; 'steam for about 40 minutes' and 'Continue to steam until cooked'.

THE UNRECONCILED DISAGREEMENTS. STEAM TIME: 20 minutes (Entsie) against 30 (here and MAGGI, which are not independent) against 40 (Aziz). LEAF: katemfe here, banana leaf or corn husk elsewhere. ALKALI: 'Salt Petre' here, 'Kanwa (Concentrated Salt)' at Prime News, and 'kanwa (potash)' in Whitby 1968. THOSE ARE THREE DIFFERENT CHEMICALS — saltpetre is potassium nitrate, kanwa is usually trona or a sodium carbonate mineral, and potash implies potassium carbonate. No source reconciles them and none is corrected.

THE OLDEST AND CLEAREST ACCOUNT, Whitby 1968, 'Foods of Ghana', verbatim: 'A northern dish. The cowpeas are ground to flour and mixed with water to a paste. A small amount of kanwa (potash...) is added to soften the flour. The paste is wrapped in leaves and steamed. It is then eaten with shea-butter and pepper. Cowpea leaves are sometimes ground and added to the beans, making bean-leaves tuubani which is green.' THAT is the source for the alkali's purpose and for the shea-butter-and-pepper serving, and it also documents a green bean-leaf variant that no modern source mentions.
A SOURCE REJECTED: ghanaianrecipes.com, with no byline and no identifiable owner, whose cue was 'firm to the touch'.
NOT FERMENTED: the bean paste is mixed and steamed immediately. No fermentation and no cue needed.
healthBenefits: Cowpea flour is high in plant protein, folate, iron and soluble fibre.
Steamed rather than fried, so very low in fat before the shea butter.
Shea butter supplies vitamins A and E.
culturalNote: Tubaani is cheap, filling and steamed in leaves, which makes it portable food for a working day in the north. The shea butter spooned over it at the end is the regional signature — shea is the northern fat the way palm oil is the southern one, and the two cuisines taste different largely because of it.
